scraped.scraped_description: If it is available we will review around two hours of CCTV footage to try to identify the incident, but it is not proportionate to review longer periods as it keeps officers from being available to respond to emergencies, visibly patrolling railway stations and trains, investigating crimes with identified lines of enquiry or which cause the most harm to victims – such as violent or sexual offences.

policy_outcomes.description: Tool created to demonstrate to British Transport Police that binary search could make reviewing longer CCTV footage feasible, challenging their two-hour footage review policy

outcome_methodology: Advocacy demonstration tool; effectiveness measured by tool performance metrics rather than policy adoption
published_performance_metrics: Tool can narrow 64 minutes of footage to 30-second window in ~10 seconds; 8-hour video search estimated at ~20 seconds
documented_limitations: Potential GDPR/privacy concerns for police use with sensitive footage
Requires user judgment to identify whether item is still present or stolen
No backend service means videos stay local but limits scalability for institutional use
failure_modes: Previous similar advocacy by computer scientists and mathematics professors to Cambridge police (2023) was unsuccessful
Police may resist adoption due to technical terminology and messenger credibility
curation_criteria: Not applicable - single developer tool without community contributions
legal_regulatory_issues: GDPR/privacy concerns regarding police use of video analysis tools
ai_involvement: Claude Code used to build the tool
political_relevance_summary: Theft Bisect addresses civic data access and transparency. A binary search tool to help identify bike theft moments in CCTV footage.

movement_building_utility.notes: Provides civic data or journalism infrastructure

generalizability_notes: Good generalizability potential — open source allows adaptation to other jurisdictions, though localization would be needed.
